24517:
Adam is the first human in the Bible's story, formed by God from the ground and placed in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. His name is also the ordinary Hebrew word for "human being," so in Genesis 1-3 he stands both as an individual and as a representative of humankind. He is made, with the woman, in the image of God and commissioned to fill and rule the earth as God's steward.

Genesis 3 tells how Adam and Eve ate from the one forbidden tree, hid from God, and were expelled from the garden. The consequences fall on work, relationships, and life itself: the ground is cursed, toil becomes hard, and death enters as a return to dust. Adam's later life is recorded only briefly: he fathers Seth and dies at 930.

In the New Testament Adam becomes a theological figure. Paul sets him against Christ as the head of an old humanity whose disobedience brought sin and death, while Christ, the "last Adam," brings righteousness and life. How literally to read Adam, and what his sin means for his descendants, are among the most discussed questions in Christian and Jewish thought.
24518: Genesis presents Adam as formed from dust and animated by God's breath (Gen 2:7), placed in Eden with a single command (Gen 2:16-17), given the woman as a partner (Gen 2:18-23), and joining her in eating the forbidden fruit (Gen 3:6). God pronounces consequences on the ground and on his labor and expels the couple (Gen 3:17-24). His genealogy lists Seth and other sons and daughters and a lifespan of 930 years (Gen 5:3-5). Luke traces Jesus' line back to Adam, "the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Paul states that sin and death entered the world through one man and that many were made sinners through his disobedience (Rom 5:12-19), and contrasts the first Adam, a living being, with the last Adam, a life-giving spirit (1 Cor 15:22, 1 Cor 15:45-49). 1 Tim 2:13-14 notes that Adam was formed first and was not deceived.
24520: Adam is the common ancestor of all people, a basis for human equality and the infinite worth of each life (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). Rabbinic thought generally speaks of the yetzer ha-ra, an inclination to evil present in every person, rather than inherited guilt; Adam's sin brought mortality but each person answers for his own deeds.
24521: Adam is a real first parent whose sin lost original holiness and justice for the whole race; all humans inherit original sin as a deprived state (not personal guilt), healed by baptism. The Church allows evolutionary accounts of the body while affirming a real primeval fall (Catechism 390, 404-405; Pius XII, *Humani Generis* 36-37).
24522: Adam's fall brought corruption and mortality into human nature; descendants inherit the condition of death and a weakened nature, but not Adam's personal guilt. Adam was created in an initial state of growth toward likeness to God, a path he abandoned and Christ restores.
24524: Adam acted as the federal (covenant) head of humanity, so that his guilt is imputed to all his descendants, just as Christ's righteousness is imputed to believers (reading Rom 5:12-21). Some evangelicals hold a recent historical Adam; others accept an ancient Adam chosen as representative within a larger population, and some read Adam as an archetype for humanity.

24533: Genesis 2-3 shares themes with ancient Near Eastern texts: humans formed from clay (Atrahasis), a lost chance at immortality (Adapa, Gilgamesh), and sacred gardens. Genesis differs in presenting one God, a good creation, and human moral responsibility rather than divine caprice. Many scholars assign Gen 2:4-3:24 to a source distinct from Gen 1:1-2:3; traditional readers see two complementary perspectives on one creation. Eden's description echoes later tabernacle and temple imagery (eastward entrance, cherubim, gold, guarding and serving), which suggests the garden is pictured as a sanctuary.

24575:
Eve is the first woman in Genesis, built by God from the man's side and greeted by him as his true counterpart. Together they bear God's image and receive the commission to fill and rule the earth. Her name, given by Adam after the fall, means "living" because she would be the mother of all living.

In Genesis 3 the serpent draws Eve into a conversation that questions God's goodness. She eats the forbidden fruit and gives it to Adam, who is with her. God's judgment includes pain in childbirth and conflict in marriage, but it also contains the promise that her offspring will strike the serpent's head, a line Christian readers have long called the first gospel.

Eve's story continues in motherhood marked by grief: she bears Cain and Abel, loses Abel to his brother's violence, and names Seth as God's replacement for the son she lost. Each birth notice records her own words about God.
24576: The woman is formed from the man's side as a "helper corresponding to him" (Gen 2:18-22); the Hebrew ʿēzer is used elsewhere of God himself (Ps 33:20), so it does not imply inferiority. She speaks with the serpent, eats, and gives to her husband "who was with her" (Gen 3:6). She says the serpent deceived her (Gen 3:13). God promises enmity between the serpent's offspring and hers (Gen 3:15) and announces painful childbearing and a desire toward her husband who will rule over her (Gen 3:16). She is named Eve (Gen 3:20) and bears Cain, Abel, and Seth (Gen 4:1-2, Gen 4:25). Paul mentions the serpent's deceiving Eve (2 Cor 11:3), and 1 Tim 2:13-14 refers to her formation after Adam and her deception.
24577: Rabbinic midrash debates whether the first human was created androgynous and then divided (Genesis Rabbah 8:1) and elaborates Eve's dialogue with the serpent, often noting that her addition of "nor touch it" shows the danger of building a fence that becomes confused with the command itself (Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 1).
24579: Since Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, Eve has been paired with Mary: Eve's disobedience is undone by Mary's obedience, making Mary the "new Eve" (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.22.4). Gen 3:15 is read as the Protoevangelium, pointing to Christ and, in Catholic tradition, to Mary's role.

24716:
Noah is the righteous man through whom God preserves life when the world is judged by the flood. Genesis describes the earth as filled with violence and God as grieved to his heart; Noah alone finds favor, walks with God, and builds the ark exactly as commanded. With his wife, three sons, their wives, and pairs of animals, he rides out the flood until the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat.

After the flood Noah offers sacrifice and God makes a covenant with him and with every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood and setting the rainbow as its sign. The command to be fruitful and multiply is renewed, making Noah a second Adam figure who heads a new humanity. From his three sons come the nations listed in Genesis 10.

The story does not end on a heroic note. Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered; the episode leads to his curse on Canaan and blessings on Shem and Japheth. Later Scripture remembers him as a model of righteousness (Ezek 14:14), of faith that acted on God's warning (Heb 11:7), and of a generation caught unprepared by judgment (Matt 24:37-39).
24717: Noah is the son of Lamech (Gen 5:28-29), called righteous and blameless in his generation (Gen 6:9). He builds the ark to God's specifications (Gen 6:14-22) and enters it at 600 years old (Gen 7:6). The flood covers the earth and the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat (Gen 7:17-8:4). God makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature, with the rainbow as sign (Gen 9:8-17). Noah becomes drunk and curses Canaan (Gen 9:20-27) and dies at 950 (Gen 9:29). Ezekiel names him with Daniel and Job as exemplary righteous men (Ezek 14:14). Jesus compares the days of Noah to the coming of the Son of Man (Matt 24:37-39). Hebrews praises his faith (Heb 11:7), 1 Peter links the flood to baptism (1 Pet 3:20-21), and 2 Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Pet 2:5).
24718: The phrase "righteous in his generation" is debated in the Talmud: one view says he would have been greater in a better generation, another that he was righteous only relative to a wicked one (b. Sanhedrin 108a). The covenant with Noah grounds the seven Noahide laws, the moral obligations rabbinic tradition sees as binding on all humanity (b. Sanhedrin 56a).
24719: The ark is a type of the Church, outside of which there is no safety, and the flood waters prefigure baptism (1 Pet 3:20-21; Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church* 6). Noah is commemorated as a righteous forefather in the Orthodox calendar.
